prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Meta Platforms, Inc." (ticker META), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "META", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Meta Platforms, Inc.
markets: Virtual/mixed reality headsets and AI smart glasses

mission.statement: Build the future of human connection and the technology that makes it possible.
mission.plain: Meta wants to make tools that help people connect with each other, from apps today to AI and glasses tomorrow.

about.plain: Meta owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger, which about 3.6 billion people use every day. The apps are free, and Meta makes money by showing ads from businesses. It also builds the Meta AI assistant, Quest virtual-reality headsets and Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.
about.customers: Mostly millions of businesses, big and small, that pay to show ads to people using its apps.
about.everyday: If you have scrolled Instagram, watched a Reel or sent a WhatsApp message, you have used Meta's products.

money.plain: Ads in Facebook, Instagram, Messenger and WhatsApp feeds and Reels
Quest VR headsets and Ray-Ban/Oakley Meta AI glasses
WhatsApp business messaging and Meta Verified subscriptions
AI assistant and Muse models, and AI agents for businesses

result.summary: Meta has a wide moat built on network effects across four apps with ~3.6 billion daily users and unmatched first-party engagement data that makes its ad targeting and measurement highly effective. Its scale lets it outspend almost anyone on AI ranking and recommendation systems, which keeps ad returns high for advertisers. The main risks are regulation, competition for attention from TikTok/YouTube and AI chatbots, and very heavy AI capital spending.

pricingPower.evidence: Through 2024-2025 Meta grew ad impressions and average price per ad at the same time (price per ad rose in most quarters, roughly mid-to-high single digits, while impressions grew ~10%+), and revenue grew 22% in 2024, 22% in 2025 and 28% year over year in Q2 2026 to $60.8B, showing advertisers keep paying more because AI-driven targeting (Advantage+) lifts their returns.

moats.evidence: Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp are among the most recognised consumer brands in the world, though the Meta corporate brand carries privacy and trust baggage.
Users' friend graphs, photos and group chats, and advertisers' pixel/Conversions API data and campaign history, make leaving costly, but attention can shift to other apps without formally leaving.
About 3.6 billion people use at least one Meta app daily (June 2026); every additional user makes WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook more valuable to other users and to advertisers seeking reach.

With ~$200B of 2025 revenue and $115B of operating cash flow, Meta can fund $130-145B of 2026 capex and custom MTIA chips, spreading AI and infrastructure costs over far more users than smaller rivals like Snap or Pinterest.
Digital advertising is large enough to support several big players (Google, Amazon, TikTok), so the market is not naturally limited to one supplier.
Meta is the incumbent and is more often the target of counter-positioning (e.g. TikTok's interest-graph feed, AI chatbots) than the beneficiary.
Years of refining ranking and ad-delivery systems (Advantage+, Andromeda, GEM ad models) and fast copying of rival formats such as Stories and Reels show strong execution know-how.
Meta's first-party behavioural data from billions of users is unique, and it has paid very large packages to hire top AI researchers into Meta Superintelligence Labs, led by Alexandr Wang.

customers.evidence: Daily active people rose to 3.60 billion in June 2026 and advertisers keep raising spend (Q2 2026 revenue +28%), but users rate Facebook poorly on satisfaction (low ACSI-style scores, privacy distrust), so loyalty is driven by habit and network rather than love.

talent.evidence: Meta pays among the highest packages in tech and lured top AI researchers in 2025, but repeated layoffs (including ~600 AI roles in late 2025), the 'year of efficiency' and reorganisations have hurt morale and its ranking on employer lists has fallen from its early-2010s peak.

product.evidence: Its ad platform is widely judged to deliver the best returns outside search, Instagram and WhatsApp lead their categories, Ray-Ban Meta glasses lead the AI glasses category and Quest leads VR headset shipments; its Llama/Muse AI models trail OpenAI, Google and Anthropic on frontier benchmarks.

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google, YouTube)
competitors.note: Digital advertising budgets, YouTube vs Reels/video, Gemini vs Meta AI, Android XR glasses

competitors.name: ByteDance (TikTok)
competitors.note: Short-form video attention and social ad budgets, especially with younger users

competitors.name: Amazon
competitors.note: Retail media and performance advertising; Alexa vs Meta AI

competitors.name: Snap
competitors.note: Messaging, Stories and AR glasses (Specs) among young users

competitors.name: Pinterest
competitors.note: Visual discovery and social commerce advertising

competitors.name: OpenAI
competitors.note: ChatGPT vs Meta AI for consumer AI assistants, future ads and devices

competitors.name: Apple
competitors.note: iMessage vs WhatsApp/Messenger, Vision Pro vs Quest, platform control over ad tracking (ATT)

competitors.name: Microsoft (LinkedIn)
competitors.note: LinkedIn social advertising; Copilot in consumer AI

competitors.name: X Corp / xAI
competitors.note: Threads vs X for real-time conversation; Grok vs Meta AI

competitors.name: Tencent
competitors.note: WeChat dominates messaging in China, where Meta's apps are blocked; competes for global gaming/social

competitors.name: Telegram
competitors.note: Messaging app competing with WhatsApp in several markets

threats: Competition for attention from TikTok, YouTube Shorts and AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, which could also become ad platforms
Regulation: EU Digital Markets Act limits on data use and 'pay or consent', US FTC antitrust case over Instagram/WhatsApp, youth-safety lawsuits and state laws
Very high AI capex ($130-145B guided for 2026) and rising expenses squeezing margins and free cash flow if AI returns disappoint
Falling behind frontier AI labs (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic) despite heavy spending on Meta Superintelligence Labs
Platform dependence on Apple and Google mobile operating systems for distribution and ad tracking
Continued Reality Labs losses of roughly $4-5B per quarter
Teen engagement shifting away from Facebook, and trust/privacy controversies

ceo.name: Mark Zuckerberg
ceo.background: Co-founded Facebook in his Harvard dorm in 2004; studied computer science and psychology at Harvard before dropping out; self-taught programmer

c1.evidence: Meta leads social media and is the No. 2 digital ad seller, which is large but maturing; it is a leader in AI glasses and VR but not in frontier AI models.

c2.evidence: Advertisers choose Meta for its unmatched reach (3.6B daily people) and AI targeting that lifts returns, and users stay because their friends and groups are there — network effects that are very hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp are household names and default leaders in social and messaging, but many users would not enthusiastically recommend Facebook given privacy and well-being concerns.

c4.evidence: Zuckerberg repeatedly stresses 'building the future of human connection' and 'personal superintelligence', but the business is overwhelmingly ad-revenue driven and the mission has shifted from 'connect the world' to metaverse to AI.

c6.evidence: “social media, privacy concerns, addictive, powerful” — the impression is mixed: people use the apps daily but the company itself is viewed with distrust.

c7.evidence: Global digital advertising (~$700B+ and growing) plus AI assistants, business messaging and smart glasses ride secular shifts to mobile, video and AI.

c8.evidence: Meta is expanding into AI assistants (Meta AI, Muse Spark), business AI agents and WhatsApp commerce, and AI wearables (Ray-Ban Meta, Meta Ray-Ban Display) — Citigroup estimates Muse alone could exceed $27B in annual revenue by 2030.

m1.evidence: Zuckerberg foresaw the shift to mobile (Instagram/WhatsApp acquisitions) and now lays out a clear vision of 'personal superintelligence' delivered through AI glasses.

m2.evidence: As founder with majority voting control, Zuckerberg makes decade-long bets such as more than $70B of cumulative Reality Labs losses and $130B+ of 2026 AI capex despite investor pushback.

m4.evidence: He is product- and user-focused, but repeated mass layoffs (about 21,000 in 2022-23) and a 'year of efficiency' show a hard-edged rather than servant leadership style.

m5.evidence: The 'move fast' hacker culture produced News Feed, Stories, Reels, Llama, Ray-Ban Meta glasses and the Andromeda/GEM ad systems.

m6.evidence: Zuckerberg is a programmer who wrote the original Facebook and personally leads AI and hardware product reviews and recruitment of AI researchers.

m7.evidence: He has pledged 99% of his Meta shares to the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative for science and education, but Meta's handling of misinformation, teen safety and privacy has drawn heavy criticism.

m7b.evidence: Mark Zuckerberg gave the Harvard University commencement address in May 2017.

m8b.evidence: Zuckerberg is one of the world's most recognisable tech founders, known for his hoodie, martial arts (jiu-jitsu) and bold public bets like the 'metaverse' rebrand.

m9.evidence: Under Zuckerberg revenue grew from near zero to $201B in 2025 with ~41% operating margin, and he executed a sharp turnaround after the 2022 downturn.

m10.evidence: The 2023 'year of efficiency' cut costs and layers, but Meta pays lavishly for AI talent and spends heavily on Reality Labs, so it is not known for frugality.

c10.evidence: WhatsApp gives billions of people, many in developing countries, free messaging and calls, and Meta's apps let small businesses reach customers cheaply.

p2.evidence: Running real-time AI ranking and messaging for 3.6B daily users is technically very hard, but social apps themselves are not unique and are seen as less essential than search or medicine.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew from $86.0B (2020) to $201.0B (2025), falling only once (-1% in 2022).

f2.evidence: Gross margin stayed around 80-82% and operating margin rose from 38% (2020) to 41% (2025), but with a dip to 29% in 2022.

f3.evidence: As of June 2026 Meta held $90.3B of cash and securities against $83.7B of long-term debt (rising fast to fund AI data centers), with strong operating cash flow ($115.8B in 2025) and positive equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $32.7B (2020) to $83.3B (2025) and operating cash flow from $38.7B to $115.8B, with a dip only in 2022.

v1.evidence: For advertisers Meta is often the best non-search channel because its targeting delivers sales cheaply, and WhatsApp/Instagram lead because everyone is on them, but rivals like TikTok and YouTube are close in engagement.

v2.evidence: Meta was long a Glassdoor Best Places to Work top-10 company (No. 1 in 2018), but it has slipped in recent rankings after layoffs and reorganisations, though pay remains top tier.

c5.evidence: Billions would miss WhatsApp and Instagram for staying in touch and small businesses would lose a cheap way to find customers, though critics argue social media harms teen mental health and spreads misinformation.
